title: The Hourglass Economy: An analysis of London's labour market
pub: London City Hall / Greater London Authority
author: London Assembly Economy Committee

dom.t: Hourglass labour: Employment growth can block progression

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source addresses London job quality, flexible-working practices and employer job design, not legal AI’s jagged capabilities, verification requirements or task-level deployment. Its discussion of operational redesign and the limits of headline metrics is broadly analogous, but it does not provide enough direct evidence to establish a position on the cluster’s proposition.

st.t: Hourglass labour: Employment growth can block progression
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: London’s employment recovery coexisted with deteriorating job quality, occupational hollowing and weaker progression into better-paid work. It also treats skills shortages and related factors as qualified explanations for weak productivity rather than establishing a single cause.
qs: We have found that, when the full picture is taken into account, London has  performed less well against these factors, between 2008 and 2015, than the  headline figures might suggest.

st.t: Job quality: Employment growth conceals unequal progression
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s proposition: it argues that headline employment growth masks insecurity, pay inequality and weak progression, while advocating procurement, Living Wage, skills and devolution reforms. It also presents several expected policy benefits as prospective rather than demonstrated outcomes.
qs: Despite growing wealth and employment, London is a highly polarised city  and suffers the greatest level of pay inequality of any region in the UK.1 The  reality is that for those who work on low-pay or with insecure contracts, have  dependent children at home, or left school with few qualifications, living and  working in London can be an everyday struggle.

In doing so, it would help the Mayor and the LEP  boost growth in new and young sectors of the economy, such as technology,  increasing the availability of quality, mid- and high-skilled jobs, and enhancing  the ability of businesses to invest in their workers and their careers.

kp.k: Headline recovery concealed deteriorating job quality
kp.d: The Committee finds that London’s post-2008 recovery produced strong growth, job creation and record employment, but these aggregate indicators obscured weaker performance in skills and productivity, job quality, inclusion and wages between 2008 and 2015. This is a cross-domain warning against treating employment totals as sufficient evidence of a healthy labour market.
qs: But dig a little deeper  …and the headline employment figures mask a reality which, for many Londoners, is far more challenging than it was before the crash.
In four areas in particular (skills and productivity; job quality; inequality; and wage growth), the underlying performance of the labour market is letting many Londoners down.

kp.k: London's labour market became increasingly hourglass-shaped
kp.d: The report identifies simultaneous growth in high- and low-skilled work alongside erosion of mid-skilled administrative, manufacturing and trade occupations. Mid-skilled occupations fell from 20 to 18 per cent of jobs between 2008 and 2015—a 13 per cent proportional decrease—while higher-skilled workforce jobs grew from 51 to 53 per cent, producing an increasingly polarised staffing structure.
qs: Concurrently, the labour market has become ‘hollowed-out’ with a 13 per  cent decline in the proportion of mid-skilled jobs over the period.

At the same time, jobs in the middle of the labour market (skilled  administrative, manufacturing and trade jobs) were increasingly hollowed out  as the proportion of jobs in occupations categorised as mid-skilled saw a 13  per cent decrease (from 20 to 18 per cent) between 2008 and 2015.
ONS figures reveal that the proportion of workforce jobs13 categorised as higher-skilled14 has grown from 51 to 53 per cent since  2008, adding further to the “hourglass” nature of London’s economy.

kp.k: Hollowing reduced progression pathways and productivity
kp.d: The Committee argues that declining mid-skilled work removed advancement routes from low-skilled employment into better-paid roles. This enlarged the pool of inexpensive low-skilled labour, weakened incentives for businesses to pursue efficiency improvements and contributed to lower productivity growth.
qs: This, in  turn, limited the opportunities for workers in the lower economic categories  to progress upward, into better paid, higher-skilled roles, thereby increasing  further the pool of available low-skilled, low-paid workers and reducing the  incentive for businesses to seek efficiencies.
When  combined with lower investment in workplace training, the result is reduced opportunities for progression of low-skilled workers into higher skilled and  better-paid jobs.

kp.k: Cheap labour discouraged automation and efficiency investment
kp.d: Ian Brinkley of the Work Foundation attributed growth in lower-skilled employment to the availability of cheap labour during the recession, which reduced employers’ need to automate or adopt technology. The report also relays the Bank of England’s view that cheap labour and weak investment in employees’ skills could impede innovation and the adoption of more efficient processes.
qs: During our investigation, we heard from Ian Brinkley, of the Work Foundation,  that the reason the relative number of lower skilled jobs in London increased  from 2008 to 2015 was that the availability of lots of cheap labour during the  recession removed the need for workforce efficiencies to be made, through  automation and technology.
Cheap labour has meant that organisations have had little incentive to  invest in operational efficiency savings.
In particular, weaker investment in ‘intangible’ capital, such as employees’ skills, may have  reduced the pace of innovation, and hindered the ability to adopt  more innovative processes.

kp.k: Outsourcing removed mid-skilled roles and internal mobility
kp.d: The GMB Union told the Committee that public-sector contracting out contributed to the loss of mid-skilled positions and progression routes. Lean contractors used fewer managers and specialists, while outsourced workers were detached from the client organisation’s pay spine; the report states that moving private-sector back-office functions away from core operations can have a similar effect.
qs: We also heard from the GMB Union, that contracting out of certain job roles in the public sector has been a significant contributor to the reduction in mid- skilled jobs, and lack of progression from low- to mid-skilled roles.
Contract companies work on a lean basis, with fewer managers and specialists,  providing very few mid-skilled roles or promotion opportunities.
Additionally,  contract workers are removed from the main pay spine of the organisation  they contract for, reducing their opportunities to progress within that  organisation.

kp.k: Labour hoarding also depressed measured productivity
kp.d: The Federation of Small Businesses suggested that employers retained trained, high-skilled workers during the downturn even when there was insufficient work, leaving them operating at around two-thirds capacity. Those workers also performed mid-skilled tasks that might otherwise have employed less-qualified workers, reducing productivity and narrowing entry and progression opportunities.
qs: It explained that redundancies were limited during the  downturn as businesses recognised the value of keeping hold of skilled,  trained staff.
However, there was less work for those in employment to do,  and so they worked at around two-thirds of their capacity.

This not only  reduced productivity, but resulted in high-skilled workers filling their time  with mid-skilled tasks which might otherwise have provided employment for  a lower-skilled or less-qualified worker.

kp.k: Skills shortages left high-skilled positions vacant
kp.d: Alongside occupational polarisation, business organisations reported insufficient labour for expanding high-skilled roles. The CBI’s 2015 education and skills survey found that 55 per cent of surveyed employers lacked confidence that they could recruit enough high-skilled employees in future; the GLA told the Committee that about 22 per cent of higher-level skilled jobs were vacant, affecting business productivity and delivery.
qs: Yet, 55 per cent of employers surveyed are “not  confident of being able to recruit sufficient high-skilled employees in future.”

“The skill system is behind the times. [Providers] deliver a high set of skills,  but they are not the skills that a particular sector would need. We have  calculated that about 22% of the higher-level skilled jobs are vacant. That is  affecting businesses’ ability to be productive and deliver.”
Separately, there  are indications that investment in basic workplace skills and training,  including in formal education, has declined.

kp.k: Flexible work expanded but often served employers
kp.d: Part-time and temporary contracts grew from 25 to 29 per cent of employment between 2008 and 2015; part-time jobs increased by 23 per cent compared with nine per cent for full-time jobs. The report distinguishes mutually beneficial quality flexibility from casual arrangements introduced to manage demand or reduce employment obligations, finding the latter concentrated at the lower end of the labour market.
qs: The proportion employed on such contracts increased  from 25 to 29 per cent between 2008 and 2015.
Figures show that,  since the recession, growth in part-time and full-time jobs was 23 per cent  and nine per cent respectively (reaching 1,583,000 and 3,991,000).

Flexibility is believed to have surged during the downturn for reasons one and  two. Jobs were made casual rather than redundant, and flexibility contributed  to the recovery, while ensuring fewer jobs were lost.

kp.k: Quality flexibility remained scarce in better-paid work
kp.d: The Timewise Foundation defined a quality flexible job as one paying more than £20,000 full-time equivalent with flexibility compatible with both employer and employee needs. Only three per cent of London vacancies above that salary level were part-time or open to flexibility—half the national average—while flexible opportunities remained concentrated in retail, hospitality and social care.
qs: The Timewise  Foundation categorises such roles, which pay a salary greater than £20,000  (full time equivalent), and have flexibility that is compatible for employee and  employer, as a ‘quality flexible job.’

“If you put a cap at £20,000 as the equivalent of a quality wage (FTE), only  three per cent of vacancies [above that level in London] are either part-time  or open to flexibility. That is half the national average.
[And] flexibility is  concentrated at the bottom of the labour market in sectors where there is  an existing need for flexibility because of customer service: retail,  hospitality and social care.”

kp.k: Casual contracts shifted insecurity onto workers
kp.d: The report finds that minimum- and zero-hours arrangements frequently provided unstable schedules, low pay and few benefits. Electronic scheduling allocated hours according to business demand, often with little notice or worker consultation; workers lacking guaranteed hours could also fear reductions in hours or tips as managerial discipline and generally lacked employee benefits such as paid holiday, sick pay and pension contributions.
qs: Hours are often allocated using  electronic scheduling systems,  and change from week to week  according to the needs of the  business (for example, demand  for hotel rooms), with little or  no warning.
This leads to high  levels of insecurity over the  hours worked, and so the pay  received, in a given period.
Finally, workers on casual, flexible contracts are generally not classed as  ‘employees’ and so don’t qualify for employer-supplied benefits such as paid  holiday, sick-pay or pension contributions.

kp.d: The Committee concludes that the scarcity of quality flexible posts reflected management attitudes as well as operational constraints. Employers were slow to redesign jobs unless flexibility delivered an immediate business benefit, despite evidence that flexible work could improve recruitment, retention, engagement, well-being and productivity.
qs: The reason these posts are not being created appears to have as much to do with management attitudes as operational constraints.
In short, where the result is not of immediate benefit to business, employers  have been slow to proactively design jobs on the basis of how, where and  when people work and want to work.
Indeed, CBI research reveals 63 per cent of employers say flexible working  practices have a positive effect on recruitment and retention.

kp.k: Occupational structures disadvantaged women and younger workers
kp.d: Women, carers and young people faced restricted access to employment, quality flexibility and progression. The employment rate for mothers and lone parents was 62 per cent compared with 71 per cent for the wider population; youth unemployment was 17.2 per cent in London versus 14.3 per cent nationally. In 2015, 24 per cent of female jobs and 49 per cent of jobs held by 18-to-24-year-olds paid below the London Living Wage.
qs: And the current  employment rate for mothers and lone parents lags behind that of the whole  population, at 62 percent compared with 71 per cent.
The unemployment rate for those aged 18 to 24 in London remains  considerably higher than the national average, at 17.2 per cent compared  with 14.3 per cent for the whole UK.

In 2015, 17 per cent of male employee jobs in London were  paid less than the London Living Wage, while 24 per cent of female employee  jobs in London and 49 per cent of employee jobs in the 18 to 24 age group in  London were paid less than the living wage

kp.k: Rigid flexibility underutilised women's existing skills
kp.d: Timewise Foundation evidence indicates that women often accepted jobs below their skill level to obtain part-time flexibility, wasting prior training and creating occupational blockages that also limited progression for less-skilled workers. It reported that 77 per cent of part-time workers became stuck in their jobs and that two-thirds of women in the UK labour market underused their skills for this reason.
qs: “77 per cent of people working part-time get stuck in their jobs”
“Two thirds of women in the UK labour market currently underutilise their  skills in the workplace, because they trade down in return for flexible part- time jobs.”
Many women returning to work have taken jobs below their skill level,  wasting prior investment in their training.

kp.k: Low pay and living costs increased poverty
kp.d: The report links wage stagnation and rising housing, childcare and transport costs to growing in-work poverty. It reports that 28 per cent of Londoners lived in low-income households compared with 21 per cent nationally, and that 57 per cent of Londoners in poverty belonged to working families. Inflation-adjusted median hourly pay for London employees aged 18 and over fell ten per cent between 2008 and 2014.
qs: London has 28 per cent of people living in a low-income  household, compared with 21 per cent nationally.
This is not limited to those  households which are out of work: 57 per cent of Londoners in poverty are  now in working families.
After adjusting for inflation, median hourly pay for employees in London aged  18 and over, fell by ten per cent between 2008 and 2014.

kp.d: The proportion of London employee jobs below the London Living Wage rose by 54 per cent between 2008 and 2015, from 13 to 20 per cent. The report cites Resolution Foundation research attributing this trend to general wage stagnation rather than increased wage-distribution inequality, and ONS data showing that 826,000 of the net 872,000 jobs added between April 2012 and April 2014—95 per cent—paid below the London Living Wage.
qs: The proportion of London’s employee  jobs earning less than the LLW increased by 54 per cent between 2008 and  2015.

Research by the Resolution Foundation43 suggests that the rising proportion  of employee jobs paid less than the LLW was due not to any increase in  inequality in the wage distribution, but rather to general wage stagnation  since the 2008 economic downturn.

The ONS Annual Survey of Hours and Earnings shows that, of the 872,000 jobs  added to the labour market between April 2012 and April 2014, a staggeringly  high proportion of the net gain (95 per cent) was in jobs paid less than the  LLW (826,000).

kp.k: Policy should measure job quality, not totals
kp.d: The Committee criticises the Mayor’s reliance on aggregate targets for full-time jobs, part-time jobs, apprenticeships and accredited Living Wage employers. It recommends routinely applying a quality metric and assessing whether jobs provide sustainable employment, fair pay, useful skills, progression and compatibility with workers’ needs.
qs: Missing from this, and evident in our analysis of the current state of the  labour market, is a quality metric, which ought to have been employed more  routinely and rigorously by the current Mayor and his team.
A new Mayor can succeed but  must move beyond a focus on summative targets for job creation, instead  driving quality in the jobs created.

For the next Mayor to avoid the issues highlighted in this report will require a renewed focus, beneath the headline figures, to ensure the jobs being  created are better tailored to the needs of London’s working population and  employers.

kp.k: Recommendations combine training, transparency, pay and flexibility
kp.d: The report recommends industry-tailored employment programmes and apprenticeships, career-advancement support for low-paid workers, sector-wide workplace-skills initiatives, employer-union action on contractual conditions, mandatory disclosure of contract and pay details in job advertisements, promotion of quality flexible hiring, and wider adoption or possible mandating of the London Living Wage.
qs: The incoming Mayor, and the LEP, should help all Londoners to compete for  better-quality jobs in the labour market, and to progress in their careers.
The incoming Mayor should work with employers and trade unions, to  improve job quality, and equalise the power balance between London’s  employees and employers.
The incoming Mayor, and the LEP, should lead by example, and speak out  publicly, to champion quality flexible working practices, and demonstrate  their importance for both employers and employees.
The next Mayor should consider the viability of mandating the LLW for  London businesses by 2020.

kp.k: Devolution could align skills with changing demand
kp.d: The Committee argues that devolving post-16 skills, apprenticeship funding, careers support, employment services and business innovation policy would allow provision to respond more rapidly to London employers’ changing needs. It presents this as a route to more relevant training, stronger career mobility and more quality mid- and high-skilled jobs, rather than as an observed result.
qs: Devolution of skills is critical.

The resulting system would deliver  outcomes-driven provision, with skills tailored to the needs of London’s  employers, and updated in a timely fashion to keep pace with the changing  needs of the economy.
Finally, devolution would enable further public investment in business  support and innovation.

In doing so, it would help the Mayor and the LEP  boost growth in new and young sectors of the economy, such as technology,  increasing the availability of quality, mid- and high-skilled jobs, and enhancing  the ability of businesses to invest in their workers and their careers.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The report makes cross-domain claims about labour-market polarisation and incentives to automate, not claims about AI or legal services.
pts.d: The Committee reports Ian Brinkley of the Work Foundation's explanation that abundant cheap labour during the recession reduced businesses' incentive to achieve efficiencies through automation and technology, contributing to growth in lower-skilled work and weaker productivity. The Committee also identifies a hollowing-out of mid-skilled administrative, manufacturing and trade roles that restricts progression from lower-paid work. It does not attribute that hollowing-out to AI: additional explanations offered by witnesses include outsourcing and skilled employees taking on mid-skilled tasks. The report's 'hourglass' describes London's occupational distribution, not a law firm's staffing structure.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence combines occupational statistics, commissioned economic analysis, employer surveys and stakeholder testimony; the automation mechanism is presented as a witness's explanation.
pts.d: The Committee draws on GLA Economics and ONS occupational data, reporting a 13 per cent relative decline in the mid-skilled share of jobs between 2008 and 2015, with rounded shares falling from 20 to 18 per cent, and a rise in the high-skilled share from 51 to 53 per cent. Its explanation concerning cheap labour and automation is attributed to Brinkley's testimony rather than an identified causal measurement. GMB supplies the outsourcing explanation, while the Federation of Small Businesses supplies the account of retained skilled staff working below capacity and absorbing mid-skilled tasks. The report also cites the Bank of England's May 2015 discussion of possible explanations for weak productivity and the CBI/Pearson 2015 survey for employer concerns and occupational forecasts. No AI-specific evidence or legal-sector evidence is offered.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The principal claims concern the post-2008 recession and recovery through 2015; cited occupational forecasts extend from 2012 to 2022.
pts.d: Published in February 2016, the report describes occupational change primarily over 2008–2015 and slower relative productivity growth over 2008–2013. Brinkley's automation explanation is conditional on the availability of cheap labour during the recession. The Committee presents several productivity mechanisms as possible explanations rather than a single established cause. For future occupational composition, it cites CBI/Pearson predictions of declines in administrative jobs and skilled trades of 13 and nine per cent respectively over 2012–2022, alongside expectations that most jobs created in that decade would be high-skilled. These are labour-market forecasts, not predictions of AI displacement.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The report identifies blocked progression for low-skilled workers and young entrants, skills underutilisation among women seeking flexible work, and recruitment constraints for employers.
pts.d: The Committee argues that fewer mid-skilled roles remove stepping stones into better-paid work, particularly for young people entering directly from school and workers in low-paid occupations. According to GMB, outsourced workers lose access to organisational pay structures and advancement opportunities. Employers face shortages of suitable high-skilled recruits despite growth in professional services, healthcare and education. Separately, the Committee and Timewise describe women accepting work below their skill level to obtain flexibility, limiting their productivity and further obstructing progression for less-skilled workers. These effects concern London's broader labour market; no effects on lawyers, legal clients or legal providers are specified.
